claim: The 12 related human ESCRT-III proteins form filaments that constrict membranes and mediate fission, including during cytokinetic abscission.
source: The 12 related human ESCRT-III proteins form filaments that constrict membranes and mediate fission, including during cytokinetic abscission.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by the manuscript's introduction and references to prior work.

claim: The C-terminal tails of polymerized ESCRT-III subunits bind proteins that contain Microtubule-Interacting and Trafficking (MIT) domains.
source: The C-terminal tails of polymerized ESCRT-III subunits also bind proteins that contain Microtubule-Interacting and Trafficking (MIT) domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the binding data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: MIT domains can interact with ESCRT-III tails in many different ways to create a complex binding code.
source: MIT domains can interact with ESCRT-III tails in many different ways to create a complex binding code that is used to recruit essential cofactors to sites of ESCRT activity.
evidence: This is supported by the description of seven different binding modes (Type 1-7) shown in Figure 1C and discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study measured 228 pairwise interactions between MIT domains and ESCRT-III tails.

claim: The study quantified 60 positive interactions between MIT domains and ESCRT-III tails.
source: We measured 228 pairwise interactions, quantified 60 positive interactions, and discovered 18 previously unreported interactions.

claim: The study discovered 18 previously unreported interactions between MIT domains and ESCRT-III tails.
source: We measured 228 pairwise interactions, quantified 60 positive interactions, and discovered 18 previously unreported interactions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and represents a novel finding of the study.

claim: The crystal structure of the SPASTIN MIT domain in complex with the IST1 C-terminal tail was determined.
source: We also report the crystal structure of the SPASTIN MIT domain in complex with the IST1 C-terminal tail.

claim: KATNA1 functions in abscission.
source: Three MIT enzymes were studied in detail and shown to: (1) localize to cytokinetic midbody membrane bridges through interactions with their specific ESCRT-III binding partners (SPASTIN-IST1, KATNA1-CHMP3, and CAPN7-IST1), (2) function in abscission (SPASTIN, KATNA1, and CAPN7)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by siRNA depletion experiments showing abscission defects in Figure 5G.

claim: CAPN7 functions in abscission.
source: Three MIT enzymes were studied in detail and shown to: (1) localize to cytokinetic midbody membrane bridges through interactions with their specific ESCRT-III binding partners (SPASTIN-IST1, KATNA1-CHMP3, and CAPN7-IST1), (2) function in abscission (SPASTIN, KATNA1, and CAPN7)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by siRNA depletion experiments showing abscission defects in Figure 5G.

claim: SPASTIN functions in the 'NoCut' abscission checkpoint.

claim: CAPN7 functions in the 'NoCut' abscission checkpoint.
source: Three MIT enzymes were studied in detail and shown to: (1) localize to cytokinetic midbody membrane bridges through interactions with their specific ESCRT-III binding partners (SPASTIN-IST1, KATNA1-CHMP3, and CAPN7-IST1), (2) function in abscission (SPASTIN, KATNA1, and CAPN7), and (3) function in the 'NoCut' abscission checkpoint (SPASTIN and CAPN7).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by checkpoint experiments in Figure 5H.

claim: Premature abscission in the presence of aberrantly segregated DNA can lead to tension-induced double strand breaks in chromatin bridges that traverse the cleavage furrow.
source: Premature abscission in the presence of aberrantly segregated DNA can lead to tension-induced double strand breaks in chromatin bridges that traverse the cleavage furrow (Janssen et al., 2011), chromosome instability (Umbreit et al., 2020), and formation of micronuclei and extensive DNA damage through chromothripsis (Zhang et al., 2015; Crasta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Janssen et al., 2011).

claim: Premature abscission can lead to chromosome instability.
source: Premature abscission in the presence of aberrantly segregated DNA can lead to tension-induced double strand breaks in chromatin bridges that traverse the cleavage furrow (Janssen et al., 2011), chromosome instability (Umbreit et al., 2020), and formation of micronuclei and extensive DNA damage through chromothripsis (Zhang et al., 2015; Crasta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Umbreit et al., 2020).

claim: Premature abscission can lead to formation of micronuclei and extensive DNA damage through chromothripsis.
source: Premature abscission in the presence of aberrantly segregated DNA can lead to tension-induced double strand breaks in chromatin bridges that traverse the cleavage furrow (Janssen et al., 2011), chromosome instability (Umbreit et al., 2020), and formation of micronuclei and extensive DNA damage through chromothripsis (Zhang et al., 2015; Crasta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zhang et al., 2015; Crasta et al., 2012).

claim: Abscission misregulation can contribute to DNA damage and cancer development.
source: Hence, abscission is required for cell proliferation and its misregulation can contribute to DNA damage and even cancer development (Pharoah et al., 2013; Sadler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Pharoah et al., 2013; Sadler et al., 2018).

claim: The ESCRT pathway mediates abscission in cultured mammalian cells.
source: The ESCRT (Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport) pathway mediates abscission in cultured mammalian cells (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007; Morita et al., 2007), and in neural progenitor cells in vivo (Tedeschi et al., 2020; Little et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007; Morita et al., 2007).

claim: The ESCRT pathway mediates abscission in neural progenitor cells in vivo.
source: The ESCRT (Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport) pathway mediates abscission in cultured mammalian cells (Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007; Morita et al., 2007), and in neural progenitor cells in vivo (Tedeschi et al., 2020; Little et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Tedeschi et al., 2020; Little et al., 2021).

claim: Approximately 30 human ESCRT factors comprise five subcomplexes: ALIX, ESCRT-I, ESCRT-II, ESCRT-III, and VPS4.
source: Approximately 30 human ESCRT factors comprise five subcomplexes: ALIX, ESCRT-I, ESCRT-II, ESCRT-III, and VPS4, which assemble sequentially to constrict and sever membranes (McCullough et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (McCullough et al., 2018).

claim: During cytokinesis, ESCRT complexes are recruited to the central Flemming body within the midbody by the CEP55 adaptor protein.
source: During cytokinesis, ESCRT complexes are recruited to the central Flemming body within the midbody by the CEP55 adaptor protein.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the following sentence to prior work on CEP55 function.

claim: CEP55 binds the early-acting ESCRT protein, ALIX.
source: CEP55 binds the early-acting ESCRT protein, ALIX (Lee et al., 2008; Christ et al., 2016; Morita et al., 2007; Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), which in turn recruits ESCRT-III subunits of the CHMP4 family (Christ et al., 2016; McCullough et al., 2008; Katoh et al., 2003; Katoh et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lee et al., 2008; Christ et al., 2016; Morita et al., 2007; Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007).

claim: ALIX recruits ESCRT-III subunits of the CHMP4 family.
source: CEP55 binds the early-acting ESCRT protein, ALIX (Lee et al., 2008; Christ et al., 2016; Morita et al., 2007; Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007), which in turn recruits ESCRT-III subunits of the CHMP4 family (Christ et al., 2016; McCullough et al., 2008; Katoh et al., 2003; Katoh et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Christ et al., 2016; McCullough et al., 2008; Katoh et al., 2003; Katoh et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2005).

claim: CEP55 binds the TSG101 subunit of ESCRT-I/II complexes.
source: In a parallel pathway, CEP55 binds the TSG101 subunit of ESCRT-I/II complexes (Morita et al., 2007; Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007; Christ et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2008), again leading to ESCRT-III recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Morita et al., 2007; Carlton and Martin-Serrano, 2007; Christ et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2008).

claim: ESCRT-III recruitment is promoted by the midbody protein SEPT9.
source: ESCRT-III recruitment is also promoted by the midbody protein SEPT9 (Karasmanis et al., 2019), and other CEP55-independent pathways (Merigliano et al., 2021; Addi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Karasmanis et al., 2019).

claim: Humans express 12 homologous ESCRT-III proteins that fall into eight different families, termed CHMP1-7 and IST1.
source: Humans express 12 homologous ESCRT-III proteins that fall into eight different families, termed CHMP1-7 and IST1.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field.

claim: Different ESCRT-III subunits co-polymerize to form spiraling filaments within the midbody.
source: The different ESCRT-III subunits co-polymerize to form spiraling filaments within the midbody (Guizetti et al., 2011; Mierzwa et al., 2017; Pfitzner et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020; Elia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Guizetti et al., 2011; Mierzwa et al., 2017; Pfitzner et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020; Elia et al., 2011).

claim: ESCRT-III filaments recruit VPS4 AAA+ ATPases that promote dynamic ESCRT-III subunit exchange, midbody constriction, membrane fission, and daughter cell separation.
source: These filaments recruit VPS4 AAA+ ATPases that in turn promote dynamic ESCRT-III subunit exchange, midbody constriction, membrane fission, and daughter cell separation (Pfitzner et al., 2021; Mierzwa et al., 2017; Elia et al., 2012; Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Pfitzner et al., 2021; Mierzwa et al., 2017; Elia et al., 2012; Pfitzner et al., 2020).

claim: The abscission/NoCut cell cycle checkpoint is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Abscission timing and progression are regulated by the evolutionarily conserved abscission/NoCut cell cycle checkpoint (Norden et al., 2006; Steigemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Norden et al., 2006; Steigemann et al., 2009).

claim: The abscission checkpoint pauses abscission progression so that upstream mitotic events can be completed correctly before the cell irreversibly separates.
source: This checkpoint pauses abscission progression so that upstream mitotic events can be completed correctly before the cell irreversibly separates.
evidence: This is a well-established function of the checkpoint supported by the cited literature.

claim: Incompletely segregated DNA within the midbody sustains abscission checkpoint activation.
source: Several different conditions are known to sustain abscission checkpoint activation, including incompletely segregated DNA within the midbody (Norden et al., 2006; Mendoza and Barral, 2008; Amaral et al., 2016), nuclear pore subunit depletion (Mackay et al., 2010), DNA damage resulting from replication stress (Mackay and Ullman, 2015), and midbody tension (Lafaurie-Janvore et al., 2013; Strohacker et al., 2021; Caballe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Norden et al., 2006; Mendoza and Barral, 2008; Amaral et al., 2016).

claim: Nuclear pore subunit depletion sustains abscission checkpoint activation.
source: Several different conditions are known to sustain abscission checkpoint activation, including incompletely segregated DNA within the midbody (Norden et al., 2006; Mendoza and Barral, 2008; Amaral et al., 2016), nuclear pore subunit depletion (Mackay et al., 2010), DNA damage resulting from replication stress (Mackay and Ullman, 2015), and midbody tension (Lafaurie-Janvore et al., 2013; Strohacker et al., 2021; Caballe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Mackay et al., 2010).

claim: DNA damage resulting from replication stress sustains abscission checkpoint activation.
source: Several different conditions are known to sustain abscission checkpoint activation, including incompletely segregated DNA within the midbody (Norden et al., 2006; Mendoza and Barral, 2008; Amaral et al., 2016), nuclear pore subunit depletion (Mackay et al., 2010), DNA damage resulting from replication stress (Mackay and Ullman, 2015), and midbody tension (Lafaurie-Janvore et al., 2013; Strohacker et al., 2021; Caballe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Mackay and Ullman, 2015).

claim: Midbody tension sustains abscission checkpoint activation.
source: Several different conditions are known to sustain abscission checkpoint activation, including incompletely segregated DNA within the midbody (Norden et al., 2006; Mendoza and Barral, 2008; Amaral et al., 2016), nuclear pore subunit depletion (Mackay et al., 2010), DNA damage resulting from replication stress (Mackay and Ullman, 2015), and midbody tension (Lafaurie-Janvore et al., 2013; Strohacker et al., 2021; Caballe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lafaurie-Janvore et al., 2013; Strohacker et al., 2021; Caballe et al., 2015).

claim: Checkpoint conditions converge on phosphorylated Aurora B (pAurB) kinase, which maintains checkpoint signaling and inhibits ESCRT activity.
source: These conditions all converge on phosphorylated Aurora B (pAurB) kinase, which maintains checkpoint signaling and inhibits ESCRT activity.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of Aurora B function and citations.

claim: Aurora B is targeted to the intercellular bridge as a component of the multi-protein Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC).
source: AurB is targeted to the intercellular bridge as a component of the multi-protein Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC), where it phosphorylates multiple substrates, including the regulatory ESCRT-III protein CHMP4C (pCHMP4C) (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012; Steigemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Aurora B phosphorylates the regulatory ESCRT-III protein CHMP4C.
source: AurB is targeted to the intercellular bridge as a component of the multi-protein Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC), where it phosphorylates multiple substrates, including the regulatory ESCRT-III protein CHMP4C (pCHMP4C) (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012; Steigemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012; Steigemann et al., 2009).

claim: Phosphorylated CHMP4C associates with ANCHR, and this complex sequesters VPS4 AAA+ ATPases from abscission sites, thereby inhibiting abscission progression.
source: pCHMP4C associates with ANCHR, and this complex sequesters VPS4 AAA+ ATPases from abscission sites, thereby inhibiting abscission progression (Thoresen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Thoresen et al., 2014).

claim: Phosphorylated Aurora B and phosphorylated CHMP4C localize to cytoplasmic Abscission Checkpoint Bodies (ACBs), where pro-abscission machinery is sequestered from the midbody.
source: pAurB and pCHMP4C also localize to cytoplasmic Abscission Checkpoint Bodies (ACBs), where pro-abscission machinery, including ALIX and ESCRT-III proteins, are sequestered from the midbody (Strohacker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Strohacker et al., 2021).

claim: A missense mutation in the penultimate CHMP4C residue (A232T) disrupts ALIX binding, inactivates the checkpoint, and predisposes carriers to several types of cancers.
source: The importance of the abscission checkpoint and its regulation by CHMP4C is underscored by the discovery that a missense mutation in the penultimate CHMP4C residue (A232T) disrupts ALIX binding, inactivates the checkpoint, and predisposes carriers to several types of cancers (Sadler et al., 2018; Pharoah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Sadler et al., 2018; Pharoah et al., 2013).

claim: Human ESCRT-III proteins have conserved helical core domains that mediate filament formation.
source: Human ESCRT-III proteins have conserved helical core domains that mediate filament formation (McCullough et al., 2018; Pfitzner et al., 2021; Bajorek et al., 2009b), and variable C-terminal tails that contain short peptide elements called MIT-Interacting Motifs (MIMs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ESCRT-III proteins have variable C-terminal tails that contain short peptide elements called MIT-Interacting Motifs (MIMs).
source: Human ESCRT-III proteins have conserved helical core domains that mediate filament formation (McCullough et al., 2018; Pfitzner et al., 2021; Bajorek et al., 2009b), and variable C-terminal tails that contain short peptide elements called MIT-Interacting Motifs (MIMs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MIT domains can bind MIM elements in at least seven distinct ways.
source: MIT domains are simple three helix bundles, but they can bind MIM elements in at least seven distinct ways (Skalicky et al., 2012; Obita et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2005; Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007; Kieffer et al., 2008, Yang et al., 2008; Solomons et al., 2011; Fujioka et al., 2014), which we have termed Type 1–7 binding modes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The tightest MIM-MIT binding pair was LIP5-CHMP5 (KD = 2.5 nM).
source: The tightest MIM-MIT binding pair was LIP5-CHMP5 (KD = 2.5 nM), which reflects the fact that CHMP5 tail helices 5 and 6 and adjacent linkers form an amphipathic 'leucine collar' that wraps almost completely around the second LIP5 MIT domain (Figure 1C; Skalicky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by binding data in Figure 2 and structural information from prior work (Skalicky et al., 2012).

claim: CHMP5 tail helices 5 and 6 and adjacent linkers form an amphipathic 'leucine collar' that wraps almost completely around the second LIP5 MIT domain.
source: The tightest MIM-MIT binding pair was LIP5-CHMP5 (KD = 2.5 nM), which reflects the fact that CHMP5 tail helices 5 and 6 and adjacent linkers form an amphipathic 'leucine collar' that wraps almost completely around the second LIP5 MIT domain (Figure 1C; Skalicky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work (Skalicky et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: IST1 bound 11/19 MIT domains with high affinity.
source: IST1 bound 11/19 MIT domains with high affinity, and this promiscuity likely reflects the presence of two MIMs in the IST1 tail; a helical Type 1 or Type 3 (Type 1/3) element (residues 344–366) and an extended Type 2 element (residues 316–343) (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Guo and Xu, 2015; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: IST1 promiscuity in MIT binding reflects the presence of two MIMs in the IST1 tail: a helical Type 1 or Type 3 element (residues 344–366) and an extended Type 2 element (residues 316–343).
source: IST1 bound 11/19 MIT domains with high affinity, and this promiscuity likely reflects the presence of two MIMs in the IST1 tail; a helical Type 1 or Type 3 (Type 1/3) element (residues 344–366) and an extended Type 2 element (residues 316–343) (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Guo and Xu, 2015; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Guo and Xu, 2015) and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The IST1 Type 1/3 element (MIM344-366) bound 10/11 MIT domains.
source: These experiments revealed that the IST1 Type 1/3 (MIM344-366) element bound 10/11 MIT domains, and the Type 2 element (MIM316-343) bound 5/11 MIT domains.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: The IST1 Type 2 element (MIM316-343) bound 5/11 MIT domains.
source: These experiments revealed that the IST1 Type 1/3 (MIM344-366) element bound 10/11 MIT domains, and the Type 2 element (MIM316-343) bound 5/11 MIT domains.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: SPASTIN, ULK3, USP8, and SPARTIN MIT domains bind only the IST1 Type 1/3 element.
source: Three binding patterns for the IST1 MIMs emerged, with MIT domains binding: (1) only the Type 1/3 element (SPASTIN, ULK3, USP8, and SPARTIN), (2) only the Type 2 element (RPS6KC1), or (3) both MIMs (VPS4A, VPS4B, CAPN7, SNX15, LIP5, and MITD1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: RPS6KC1 MIT domain binds only the IST1 Type 2 element.
source: Three binding patterns for the IST1 MIMs emerged, with MIT domains binding: (1) only the Type 1/3 element (SPASTIN, ULK3, USP8, and SPARTIN), (2) only the Type 2 element (RPS6KC1), or (3) both MIMs (VPS4A, VPS4B, CAPN7, SNX15, LIP5, and MITD1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: VPS4A, VPS4B, CAPN7, SNX15, LIP5, and MITD1 MIT domains bind both IST1 MIM elements.
source: Three binding patterns for the IST1 MIMs emerged, with MIT domains binding: (1) only the Type 1/3 element (SPASTIN, ULK3, USP8, and SPARTIN), (2) only the Type 2 element (RPS6KC1), or (3) both MIMs (VPS4A, VPS4B, CAPN7, SNX15, LIP5, and MITD1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: A fluorescently labeled CHMP4C peptide did not bind detectably to any MIT domain tested.
source: At the other end of the spectrum, a fluorescently labeled CHMP4C peptide did not bind detectably to any MIT domain tested.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: CHMP4C contains a serine-rich insertion that is phosphorylated by Aurora B.
source: CHMP4C is unique in containing a serine-rich insertion that is phosphorylated by AurB (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: CHMP4C bound AMSH MIT with a Ki of 14 µM.
source: These experiments revealed that CHMP4C bound AMSH MIT (Ki 14 µM), but still failed to bind MITD1 or USP8.
evidence: This is supported by competition binding data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: CHMP4C performs a unique role in abscission checkpoint regulation.
source: CHMP4C performs a unique role in abscission checkpoint regulation (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012), and this specialized function may have relieved the selective pressure to maintain some MIT binding interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Carlton et al., 2012; Capalbo et al., 2012).

claim: ULK1(MIT)2 did not bind detectably to any of the ESCRT-III binding partners of ULK3.
source: However, ULK1(MIT)2 did not bind detectably to any of the ESCRT-III binding partners of ULK3, implying that these ESCRT-III interactions are not conserved in the ULK family of protein kinases.
evidence: This is supported by pulldown data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: ESCRT-III interactions are not conserved in the ULK family of protein kinases.
source: However, ULK1(MIT)2 did not bind detectably to any of the ESCRT-III binding partners of ULK3, implying that these ESCRT-III interactions are not conserved in the ULK family of protein kinases.
evidence: This is inferred from the pulldown data showing ULK1 does not bind ESCRT-III proteins while ULK3 does.

claim: SPASTIN and KATNA1 are microtubule severing AAA+ ATPases.
source: SPASTIN and KATNA1 are microtubule severing AAA+ ATPases (Sharp and Ross, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Sharp and Ross, 2012).

claim: SPASTIN and KATNA1 have been implicated in clearing midbody microtubules prior to abscission.
source: Both have been implicated in clearing midbody microtubules prior to abscission (Yang et al., 2008; Connell et al., 2009; Benz et al., 2012; Matsuo et al., 2013), but neither has been linked to abscission checkpoint activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Yang et al., 2008; Connell et al., 2009; Benz et al., 2012; Matsuo et al., 2013).

claim: CAPN7 is an understudied cysteine protease that has not previously been linked to any cytokinetic functions.
source: CAPN7 is an understudied cysteine protease that has not previously been linked to any cytokinetic functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The SPASTIN MIT-IST1 complex structure was determined at 1.15 Å resolution.
source: We determined a high resolution (1.15 Å) crystal structure of the SPASTIN MIT-IST1 complex using a SPASTIN MIT112-196 construct. (Figure 4A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, and Supplementary file 3; PDB 7S7J).
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data in Supplementary file 3 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The IST1 MIM344-366 adopts an amphipathic helix that buries its hydrophobic side chains in the SPASTIN MIT H1/H3 groove (Type 3 binding).
source: The structure revealed that the IST1 MIM344-366 adopts an amphipathic helix that buries its hydrophobic side chains in the SPASTIN MIT H1/H3 groove (Type 3 binding, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IST1 and CHMP1B MIM elements exhibit similar binding modes to SPASTIN MIT.
source: The IST1 and CHMP1B MIM elements exhibit similar binding modes (Figure 4A–D), but with two significant differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C): (1) The longer CHMP1B helix extends three additional turns beyond the IST1 N-terminus, and (2) the MIT H1/H3 groove expands to accommodate the longer CHMP1B helix, with a maximal displacement of 2.5 Å at the N-terminus of helix 3.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The structure of SPASTIN-IST1 is nearly identical to SPARTIN-IST1.
source: The structure of SPASTIN-IST1 is nearly identical to SPARTIN-IST1, which also adopts a Type 3 interaction (Guo and Xu, 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and citation to prior work (Guo and Xu, 2015).

claim: IST1 binding to SPASTIN is slightly tighter than CHMP1B binding, likely owing to enhanced hydrophobic interactions with the SPASTIN H1/H3 groove.
source: IST1 binding is slightly tighter than CHMP1B binding, likely owing to enhanced hydrophobic interactions with the SPASTIN H1/H3 groove (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 2 and structural analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IST1 buries two aromatic and two aliphatic side chains in the SPASTIN H1/H3 groove, whereas CHMP1B lacks aromatic residues and buries only three aliphatics.
source: IST1 buries two aromatic and two aliphatic side chains, whereas the CHMP1B binding element lacks aromatic residues and buries only three aliphatics.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SPASTIN F124D mutation disrupts binding to both CHMP1B and IST1.
source: Based on our structural analyses, we created SPASTIN MIT mutations designed to disrupt the binding of both CHMP1B and IST1 (F124D, red in Figure 4A–D) and to disrupt only CHMP1B binding without affecting IST1 binding (L177D, cyan in Figure 4A–D). As shown in Figure 4E and F, these mutations behaved as designed
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The SPASTIN L177D mutation disrupts only CHMP1B binding without affecting IST1 binding.
source: Based on our structural analyses, we created SPASTIN MIT mutations designed to disrupt the binding of both CHMP1B and IST1 (F124D, red in Figure 4A–D) and to disrupt only CHMP1B binding without affecting IST1 binding (L177D, cyan in Figure 4A–D). As shown in Figure 4E and F, these mutations behaved as designed
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: CHMP3 binding was inhibited by both SPASTIN F124D and L177D mutants.
source: CHMP3 binding was also inhibited by both SPASTIN F124D and L177D mutants.
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CHMP3 likely binds as an extended Type 3 helix in the SPASTIN MIT H1/H3 groove.
source: Thus, CHMP3 also likely binds as an extended Type 3 helix in the SPASTIN MIT H1/H3 groove (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and only IST1 retained binding to the SPASTIN L177D mutant owing to its shorter Type 3 helix.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing both F124D and L177D disrupt CHMP3 binding.

claim: The KATNA1 V55D mutation eliminated CHMP3 binding.
source: In the KATNA1-CHMP3 case, a point mutation in the MIT H1/H3 groove (V55D) eliminated CHMP3 binding (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 4G.

claim: CHMP3 MIM element forms a Type 3 interaction with KATNA1 MIT.
source: Our data therefore again indicate a Type 3 interaction for the helical CHMP3 MIM element.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing V55D in the H1/H3 groove disrupts binding.

claim: IST1 binding to CAPN7 was significantly reduced (~30–70 fold) by point mutations in the H1/H3 groove of either the first (V18D) or second (F98D) CAPN7 MIT domains.
source: CAPN7 has tandem MIT domains, and we found that IST1 binding was significantly reduced (~30–70 fold) by point mutations in the H1/H3 groove of either the first (V18D) or second (F98D) CAPN7 MIT domains (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 4H.

claim: Both CAPN7 MIT domains engage both IST1 MIM elements, employing Type 2 (MIM316-343) and Type 3 (MIM344-366) binding modes.
source: Together with our MIM mapping experiments (Figure 3C), these data indicate that both CAPN7 MIT domains engage both IST1 MIM elements, employing Type 2 (MIM316-343) and Type 3 (MIM344-366) binding modes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of MIM mapping data (Figure 3C) and mutagenesis data (Figure 4H).

claim: Endogenous SPASTIN localizes to midbodies of dividing cells.
source: As an initial screen for cytokinetic functions, we examined whether endogenous SPASTIN, KATNA1, and/or CAPN7 localize to the midbodies of dividing cells (Figure 5A–C, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A.

claim: Endogenous KATNA1 localizes to midbodies of dividing cells.
source: As an initial screen for cytokinetic functions, we examined whether endogenous SPASTIN, KATNA1, and/or CAPN7 localize to the midbodies of dividing cells (Figure 5A–C, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B.

claim: Endogenous CAPN7 localizes to midbodies of dividing cells.
source: As an initial screen for cytokinetic functions, we examined whether endogenous SPASTIN, KATNA1, and/or CAPN7 localize to the midbodies of dividing cells (Figure 5A–C, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: SPASTIN, KATNA1, and CAPN7 co-localized with CEP55 ring structures on either side of the Flemming body.
source: In midbody-containing cells, all three MIT proteins co-localized with CEP55 ring structures on either side of the Flemming body (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A-C.

claim: KATNA1 distributed along the midbody arms, reminiscent of localization observed for caveolae, termed 'midbody entry points'.
source: Uniquely, KATNA1 also distributed along the midbody arms, reminiscent of localization observed for caveolae, and termed 'midbody entry points' (Andrade et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B and citation to prior work (Andrade et al., 2022).

claim: KATNA1 arm staining was particularly prominent in early midbody-stage cells.
source: Arm staining was particularly prominent in early midbody-stage cells (Figure 5B), and a similar KATNA1 staining pattern has been reported in rat cell lines (Matsuo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B and citation to prior work (Matsuo et al., 2013).

claim: This is the first report that CAPN7 localizes to midbodies.
source: Importantly ours is the first report that CAPN7 localizes to midbodies.
evidence: This is a novel finding of the study supported by the localization data in Figure 5C.

claim: Under checkpoint active conditions, SPASTIN, KATNA1, and CAPN7 localized to Flemming bodies with more diffuse staining and spreading to midbody arms.
source: In all cases, the MIT proteins again localized to Flemming bodies, although in each case abscission checkpoint signaling led to more diffuse staining and spreading of the signals to midbody arms.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Cells lacking KATNA1 showed strong abscission failure phenotypes, with near doubling of the percentages of cells with midbodies or multiple nuclei.
source: Cells lacking KATNA1 and CAPN7 both showed strong abscission failure phenotypes, with near doubling of the percentages of cells with midbodies or multiple nuclei (vs. control cells transfected with non-targeting (NT) siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5G.

claim: Cells lacking CAPN7 showed strong abscission failure phenotypes, with near doubling of the percentages of cells with midbodies or multiple nuclei.
source: Cells lacking KATNA1 and CAPN7 both showed strong abscission failure phenotypes, with near doubling of the percentages of cells with midbodies or multiple nuclei (vs. control cells transfected with non-targeting (NT) siRNA).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5G.

claim: The abscission defects from KATNA1 and CAPN7 depletion resembled those observed with moderate knockdown of IST1.
source: These pronounced phenotypes resembled the abscission defects observed with moderate knockdown of the essential IST1 protein (positive control) (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Agromayor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of quantification data in Figure 5G and citations to prior work.

claim: Cells lacking SPASTIN exhibited significant but weaker abscission defects compared to KATNA1 and CAPN7 depletion.
source: Cells lacking SPASTIN also exhibited significant abscission defects, although the effects were weaker.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5G.

claim: Co-depletion of SPASTIN with nucleoporins significantly reduced midbody accumulation during checkpoint activation.
source: However, simultaneous co-depletion of either SPASTIN or CAPN7 significantly reduced midbody accumulation, indicating roles for both proteins in abscission checkpoint maintenance (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5H.

claim: Co-depletion of CAPN7 with nucleoporins significantly reduced midbody accumulation during checkpoint activation.
source: However, simultaneous co-depletion of either SPASTIN or CAPN7 significantly reduced midbody accumulation, indicating roles for both proteins in abscission checkpoint maintenance (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5H.

claim: The effects of depleting SPASTIN or CAPN7 on checkpoint maintenance were at least as penetrant as depleting CHMP4C.
source: Indeed, the effects of depleting either SPASTIN or CAPN7 were at least as penetrant as depleting CHMP4C (positive control), which plays a well-characterized role in inhibiting abscission in response to checkpoint signaling (Capalbo et al., 2012; Carlton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5H and citations to prior work.

claim: KATNA1 depletion did not significantly alter midbody numbers during checkpoint activation.
source: Unlike SPASTIN or CAPN7 depletion, KATNA1 depletion did not significantly alter midbody numbers, although a second oligo targeting KATNA1 showed a modest but significant decrease in cells undergoing an abscission checkpoint arrest (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SPASTIN F124D mutant did not localize to midbodies.
source: Strikingly, however, the F124D mutant did not localize to midbodies.
evidence: This is supported by localization data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: ESCRT-III binding is required to localize SPASTIN to the midbody.
source: These data imply that ESCRT-III binding is required to localize SPASTIN to the midbody.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the F124D mutant, which disrupts ESCRT-III binding, does not localize to midbodies.

claim: CHMP1B and CHMP3 binding are dispensable for SPASTIN midbody localization when IST1 binding capability is maintained.
source: The SPASTIN F124D mutation disrupts binding to CHMP1B, IST1, and CHMP3 whereas the L177D mutation selectively permits only IST1 binding (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Therefore, our data imply that CHMP1B and CHMP3 binding are dispensable for midbody localization when IST1 binding capability is maintained.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the L177D mutant, which only binds IST1, still localizes to midbodies.

claim: The KATNA1 MIT domain binds the C-terminal domain of the KATNB1 subunit to form the KATNA1 holoenzyme.
source: The KATNA1 MIT domain binds the C-terminal domain of the KATNB1 subunit to form the KATNA1 holoenzyme (Faltova et al., 2019; Rezabkova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Faltova et al., 2019; Rezabkova et al., 2017).

claim: KATNB1 activates and localizes KATNA1 to centrosomes where it severs mitotic spindle microtubules.
source: KATNB1 activates and localizes KATNA1 to centrosomes where it severs mitotic spindle microtubules (Matsuo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Matsuo et al., 2013).

claim: KATNB1 does not appear to be responsible for localizing KATNA1 for cytokinesis function, as the two proteins do not co-localize within the midbody.
source: However, KATNB1 does not appear to be responsible for localizing KATNA1 for cytokinesis function, as the two proteins reportedly do not co-localize within the midbody (Matsuo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Matsuo et al., 2013).

claim: The KATNA1 V55D mutant does not localize to midbodies.
source: Our localization data demonstrate that WT mCherry-KATNA1 localizes to Flemming bodies and midbody arms, but the V55D mutant does not (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by localization data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: CHMP3 is the sole ESCRT-III binding partner of KATNA1.
source: CHMP3 is the sole ESCRT-III binding partner of KATNA1, and the V55D mutation disrupts this partnership (Figure 3), implying that CHMP3 localizes KATNA1 to the midbody for abscission.
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 3.

claim: CHMP3 localizes KATNA1 to the midbody for abscission.
source: CHMP3 is the sole ESCRT-III binding partner of KATNA1, and the V55D mutation disrupts this partnership (Figure 3), implying that CHMP3 localizes KATNA1 to the midbody for abscission.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the V55D mutant, which disrupts CHMP3 binding, does not localize to midbodies.

claim: The KATNA1 V55D mutation does not disrupt KATNB1 binding.
source: This was not the case, however, as KATNB1 co-precipitated with full length KATNA1 WT and V55D mutant proteins equally well from HEK293T cell extracts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-precipitation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The KATNA1 V55D mutation discriminates between CHMP3 and KATNB1 binding.
source: Hence, our data imply that the KATNA1 V55D mutation discriminates between CHMP3 and KATNB1 binding, and therefore that CHMP3 is likely responsible for localizing KATNA1 to Flemming bodies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that V55D disrupts CHMP3 binding but not KATNB1 binding.

claim: CHMP3 localizes to Flemming bodies.
source: Consistent with this model, CHMP3 localizes to Flemming bodies (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Dukes et al., 2008), and its depletion increases the propensity of cells to develop multiple nuclei and midbody bridges (Morita et al., 2010), thereby phenocopying KATNA1 loss (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Dukes et al., 2008).

claim: CHMP3 depletion increases the propensity of cells to develop multiple nuclei and midbody bridges, phenocopying KATNA1 loss.
source: Consistent with this model, CHMP3 localizes to Flemming bodies (Mierzwa et al., 2017; Dukes et al., 2008), and its depletion increases the propensity of cells to develop multiple nuclei and midbody bridges (Morita et al., 2010), thereby phenocopying KATNA1 loss (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Morita et al., 2010) and comparison to data in Figure 5G.

claim: A point mutation in the second CAPN7 MIT domain (F98D) that decreased IST1 binding ~30-fold also potently suppressed CAPN7 targeting to the Flemming body.
source: Finally, our MIT screening data suggested that IST1 could be responsible for localizing CAPN7 to midbodies (Figure 2). In support of this model, a point mutation in the second CAPN7 MIT domain that decreased IST1 binding ~30-fold (F98D, see Figure 3) also potently suppressed CAPN7 targeting to the Flemming body (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by binding data in Figure 3 and localization data in Figure 6E and F.

claim: IST1 is responsible for localizing CAPN7 to midbodies.
source: Finally, our MIT screening data suggested that IST1 could be responsible for localizing CAPN7 to midbodies (Figure 2). In support of this model, a point mutation in the second CAPN7 MIT domain that decreased IST1 binding ~30-fold (F98D, see Figure 3) also potently suppressed CAPN7 targeting to the Flemming body (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the F98D mutant, which disrupts IST1 binding, does not localize to midbodies.

claim: Most human MIT domains can mediate ESCRT-III binding.
source: We found that most human MIT domains can mediate ESCRT-III binding, further implicating MIT proteins as a major class of ESCRT pathway cofactors.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive binding data in Figure 2.

claim: The primary biological function of MIT domains is to localize proteins to sites of ESCRT-driven membrane remodeling.
source: Together with previous studies, our work indicates that the primary biological function of MIT domains is to localize proteins to sites of ESCRT-driven membrane remodeling.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data in Figures 5 and 6 and prior knowledge in the field.

claim: MIT domains have evolved to mediate protein-protein interactions in autophagosome initiation.
source: MIT domains have also evolved to mediate protein-protein interactions in other pathways, most notably in autophagosome initiation (Fujioka et al., 2014; Young et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Fujioka et al., 2014; Young et al., 2019).

claim: Polymerization of ESCRT-III creates the potential for high avidity binding with MIT domains.
source: Although we studied the pairwise interactions of MIT domains and ESCRT-III tails, these interactions likely occur predominantly in the context of polymeric ESCRT-III filaments. Polymerization creates the potential for high avidity binding, and variations in ESCRT-III subunit compositions can alter binding modes and tune binding affinities.
evidence: This is inferred from the known polymeric nature of ESCRT-III and principles of multivalent binding.

claim: Variations in ESCRT-III subunit compositions can alter binding modes and tune binding affinities with MIT domains.
source: Although we studied the pairwise interactions of MIT domains and ESCRT-III tails, these interactions likely occur predominantly in the context of polymeric ESCRT-III filaments. Polymerization creates the potential for high avidity binding, and variations in ESCRT-III subunit compositions can alter binding modes and tune binding affinities.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of binding modes and affinities observed in the study.

claim: ESCRT-III subunit compositions change as filaments mature and constrict membranes.
source: These properties are important because subunit compositions change as filaments mature and constrict membranes (Pfitzner et al., 2021; Banjade et al., 2021; Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Pfitzner et al., 2021; Banjade et al., 2021; Pfitzner et al., 2020).

claim: CHMP6 initially nucleates the assembly of ESCRT-III strands composed of CHMP4 subunits.
source: Current models for ESCRT-III assembly, derived from studies in simpler yeast systems, hold that CHMP6 initially nucleates the assembly of ESCRT-III strands composed of CHMP4 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to yeast studies.

claim: CHMP4 strands recruit partner strands composed of CHMP2/CHMP3 subunits.
source: CHMP4 strands then recruit partner strands composed of CHMP2/CHMP3 subunits (Teis et al., 2008; Babst et al., 2002), which are subsequently exchanged for CHMP1/IST1 subunits (Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Teis et al., 2008; Babst et al., 2002).

claim: CHMP2/CHMP3 subunits are subsequently exchanged for CHMP1/IST1 subunits.
source: CHMP4 strands then recruit partner strands composed of CHMP2/CHMP3 subunits (Teis et al., 2008; Babst et al., 2002), which are subsequently exchanged for CHMP1/IST1 subunits (Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pfitzner et al., 2020).

claim: The cadre of recruited MIT protein binding partners may evolve as ESCRT-III filaments mature.
source: Hence, the cadre of recruited MIT protein binding partners may evolve as filaments mature.
evidence: This is inferred from the changing subunit composition during filament maturation and the different binding specificities observed.

claim: VPS4 enzymes and LIP5 form 'supercomplexes' that display 30 MIT domains.
source: These different principles are nicely illustrated by VPS4 enzymes and their associated activator LIP5 (Vta1 in yeast), which form 'supercomplexes' that display 30 MIT domains; six from the VPS4 hexamer and 24 from the 12 associated LIP5(MIT)2 elements (Skalicky et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Skalicky et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012).

claim: VPS4 MIT domains bind promiscuously to many ESCRT-III tails.
source: VPS4 MIT domains bind promiscuously to many ESCRT-III tails, and although binding is often weak avidity effects can presumably create high affinity binding.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: VPS4A MIT binds with three- to 20-fold higher affinities than VPS4B MIT to CHMP1, CHMP2 and IST1.
source: We measured strong to moderate, Type 1 VPS4 MIT binding to the late- acting CHMP1, CHMP2 and IST1 subunits (nM to mid-μM KDs), with three- to 20-fold higher affinities consistently seen for VPS4A MIT vs. VPS4B MIT.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: VPS4 remodeling activity increases as ESCRT-III filaments mature and accumulate increasing fractions of late-acting CHMP2, CHMP1, and IST1 subunits.
source: Moreover, their different binding affinities can explain why VPS4 remodeling activity increases as ESCRT-III filaments mature and accumulate increasing fractions of the late-acting, and higher affinity CHMP2, CHMP1, and IST1 subunits (Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data and supported by citation to prior work (Pfitzner et al., 2020).

claim: IST1, CHMP3, and CHMP1 were the most promiscuous ESCRT-III binders in the screen.
source: It is therefore of interest that IST1, CHMP3, and CHMP1 were the most promiscuous ESCRT-III binders in our screen because each of these ESCRT-III subunits functions at transitional stages of ESCRT-III polymer maturation (Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: IST1, CHMP3, and CHMP1 function at transitional stages of ESCRT-III polymer maturation.
source: It is therefore of interest that IST1, CHMP3, and CHMP1 were the most promiscuous ESCRT-III binders in our screen because each of these ESCRT-III subunits functions at transitional stages of ESCRT-III polymer maturation (Pfitzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Pfitzner et al., 2020).

claim: Many MIT proteins will bind best to mature, IST1-containing filaments that form late, when membrane constriction is greatest and fission is most imminent.
source: Our binding data suggest that many MIT proteins will bind best to mature, IST1-containing filaments that form late, when membrane constriction is greatest and fission is most imminent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IST1 is the most promiscuous binder and binds many MIT domains with high affinity.

claim: AMSH and MITD1 bind many different ESCRT-III subunits with similar affinities.
source: In contrast, MIT proteins like AMSH and MITD1 bind many different ESCRT-III subunits with similar affinities, perhaps because deubiquitination (AMSH) and midbody stabilization (MITD1) are required throughout abscission and other ESCRT-dependent processes.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: Deubiquitination by AMSH and midbody stabilization by MITD1 are required throughout abscission and other ESCRT-dependent processes.
source: In contrast, MIT proteins like AMSH and MITD1 bind many different ESCRT-III subunits with similar affinities, perhaps because deubiquitination (AMSH) and midbody stabilization (MITD1) are required throughout abscission and other ESCRT-dependent processes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the promiscuous binding patterns observed.

claim: IST1 is the most promiscuous MIT binding ESCRT-III protein.
source: IST1 is the most promiscuous MIT binding ESCRT-III protein, and it binds most targets with high affinity (Figure 2, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2 and Figure 3C.

claim: IST1 promiscuity is achieved through combined use of two different MIM elements and through multi-modal binding by the IST1 MIM1/3 element.
source: IST1 promiscuity is achieved through combined use of two different MIM elements, and through multi-modal binding by the IST1 MIM1/3 element (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Guo and Xu, 2015; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3 and citations to prior work (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Guo and Xu, 2015).

claim: Both IST1 MIM elements can mediate MIT-binding, and they often collaborate to enhance binding.
source: Our screen revealed that both IST1 MIM elements can mediate MIT-binding, and that they often collaborate to enhance binding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 3C.

claim: The IST1 MIM344-366 element can make Type 3 MIT interactions.
source: The SPASTIN MIT-IST1 structure shows that the IST1 MIM344-366 element can make Type 3 MIT interactions, as seen previously in the SPARTIN-MIT-IST1 complex (Yang et al., 2008; Guo and Xu, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data in Figure 4 and citations to prior work.

claim: The same hydrophobic surface of the IST1 MIM344-366 helix can form Type 1 interactions with the MIT domains of ULK3, VPS4B, and LIP5.
source: However, the same hydrophobic surface of the IST1 MIM344-366 helix can also form Type 1 interactions with the MIT domains of ULK3, VPS4B, and LIP5 (Guo and Xu, 2015; Skalicky et al., 2012; Caballe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work (Guo and Xu, 2015; Skalicky et al., 2012; Caballe et al., 2015).

claim: IST1 depletion induces severe cytokinetic defects.
source: IST1 depletion induces severe cytokinetic defects (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Agromayor et al., 2009; Figure 5), reflecting its central role in abscission and as a versatile hub for MIT cofactor recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Agromayor et al., 2009) and data in Figure 5.

claim: IST1 has a central role in abscission and serves as a versatile hub for MIT cofactor recruitment.
source: IST1 depletion induces severe cytokinetic defects (Bajorek et al., 2009a, Agromayor et al., 2009; Figure 5), reflecting its central role in abscission and as a versatile hub for MIT cofactor recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the severe phenotype upon depletion and the promiscuous binding to many MIT domains.

claim: IST1 binding is sufficient for SPASTIN midbody recruitment.
source: This SPASTIN mutant still localized to intercellular bridges (Figure 6A,B) demonstrating that IST1 binding is sufficient (and CHMP1B and CHMP3 are dispensable) for midbody recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by localization data in Figure 6A and B showing the L177D mutant (which only binds IST1) still localizes to midbodies.

claim: SPASTIN midbody localization is impaired by CHMP1B depletion because IST1 recruitment is affected by the absence of CHMP1B.
source: Others have reported that SPASTIN midbody localization is impaired by CHMP1B depletion (Yang et al., 2008), but this observation can be reconciled because IST1 recruitment is also likely affected by the absence of CHMP1B (Dimaano et al., 2008; Rue et al., 2008; Bajorek et al., 2009b, Goliand et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from citations to prior work showing IST1 recruitment depends on CHMP1B (Dimaano et al., 2008; Rue et al., 2008; Bajorek et al., 2009b, Goliand et al., 2018).

claim: CHMP1B and CHMP3 are promiscuous MIT binders.
source: CHMP1B and CHMP3 are also promiscuous MIT binders.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: CHMP1B binds two MIT domains (SPASTIN, USP8) that the closely related CHMP1A protein does not.
source: CHMP1B binds two MIT domains (SPASTIN, USP8) that the closely related CHMP1A protein does not.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: CHMP1B's expanded binding range reflects the ability to access the Type 3 interaction mode.
source: This expanded binding range apparently reflects the ability of CHMP1B to access the Type 3 interaction mode.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing CHMP1B forms a Type 3 interaction with SPASTIN.

claim: The Type 3 interaction extends the N-terminus of the CHMP1B MIM helix by three additional turns vs. its Type 1 interactions.
source: The Type 3 interaction extends the N-terminus of the CHMP1B MIM helix by three additional turns (vs. its Type 1 interactions).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: USP8 MIT domain can discriminate between CHMP1B and CHMP1A.
source: The USP8 MIT domain can also discriminate between CHMP1B and CHMP1A (Figure 2), and we therefore speculate that USP8 MIT may also form a Type 3 interaction with CHMP1B.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: USP8 MIT may form a Type 3 interaction with CHMP1B.
source: The USP8 MIT domain can also discriminate between CHMP1B and CHMP1A (Figure 2), and we therefore speculate that USP8 MIT may also form a Type 3 interaction with CHMP1B.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similarity to SPASTIN binding.

claim: The CHMP3 MIM element can bind in at least two separate grooves of different MIT domains.
source: The CHMP3 MIM appears to be another example of a promiscuous helical MIM element that can bind in at least two separate grooves of different MIT domains.
evidence: This is supported by the binding data and structural information from prior work.

claim: The CHMP3 MIM element binds the MIT domains of AMSH using a Type 4 mode.
source: The CHMP3 MIM element binds the MIT domains of AMSH using a Type 4 mode (Figure 1C; Solomons et al., 2011), and LIP5 (MIT1 using a Type1/4 mode; Skalicky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work (Solomons et al., 2011).

claim: The CHMP3 MIM element binds LIP5 MIT1 using a Type1/4 mode.
source: The CHMP3 MIM element binds the MIT domains of AMSH using a Type 4 mode (Figure 1C; Solomons et al., 2011), and LIP5 (MIT1 using a Type1/4 mode; Skalicky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work (Skalicky et al., 2012).

claim: CHMP3 can adopt a Type 3 binding mode with SPASTIN and KATNA1 MIT domains.
source: Remarkably, our study suggests that CHMP3 can also adopt yet another binding mode (Type 3), as we mapped binding to the H1/H3 grooves of SPASTIN and KATNA1 MIT.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing mutations in the H1/H3 groove disrupt CHMP3 binding.

claim: The ability to adopt multiple different binding modes increases the number of possible partnerships with MIT domain proteins.
source: The ability to adopt multiple different binding modes increases the number of possible partnerships with MIT domain proteins, and helps to explain why IST1, CHMP3 and CHMP1B are the most promiscuous MIT binders.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins can bind in multiple modes and are the most promiscuous binders.

claim: ESCRT-III proteins coordinate the recruitment of the microtubule severing enzymes KATNA1 and SPASTIN to complete abscission.
source: ESCRT-III proteins coordinate the recruitment of the microtubule severing enzymes KATNA1 and SPASTIN to complete abscission.
evidence: This is supported by the localization and functional data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Densely packed midbody microtubules must be cleared from the midbody to facilitate cytokinetic membrane abscission.
source: Following anaphase, densely packed midbody microtubules must be cleared from the midbody to facilitate cytokinetic membrane abscission (Sharp and Ross, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Sharp and Ross, 2012).

claim: SPASTIN and KATNA1 form hexameric rings that can engage the C-terminal tails of TUBULIN subunits within the central pore.
source: Both SPASTIN and KATNA1 form hexameric rings (Hartman and Vale, 1999; Eckert et al., 2012) that can engage the C-terminal tails of TUBULIN subunits within the central pore (Kuo and Howard, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hartman and Vale, 1999; Eckert et al., 2012; Kuo and Howard, 2021).

claim: ATP hydrolysis drives polypeptide translocation by SPASTIN and KATNA1, promoting subunit exchange and/or microtubule severing.
source: ATP hydrolysis then drives polypeptide translocation, thereby promoting subunit exchange and/or microtubule severing (Roll-Mecak and Vale, 2008; Zehr et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Roll-Mecak and Vale, 2008; Zehr et al., 2017).

claim: SPASTIN and KATNA1 exhibit distinct but overlapping midbody localization patterns.
source: We observed distinct but overlapping midbody localization patterns for SPASTIN and KATNA1 (Figure 5), which may reflect their recruitment by similar ESCRT-III proteins (CHMP1B, IST1, and CHMP3) and could allow the two enzymes to act on different pools of midbody microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by the localization data in Figure 5.

claim: The distinct localization patterns of SPASTIN and KATNA1 may allow the two enzymes to act on different pools of midbody microtubules.
source: We observed distinct but overlapping midbody localization patterns for SPASTIN and KATNA1 (Figure 5), which may reflect their recruitment by similar ESCRT-III proteins (CHMP1B, IST1, and CHMP3) and could allow the two enzymes to act on different pools of midbody microtubules.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed localization patterns.

claim: SPASTIN, but not necessarily KATNA1, is required for abscission checkpoint maintenance.
source: Our discovery that SPASTIN, but not necessarily KATNA1, is required for abscission checkpoint maintenance further underscores that these enzymes likely mediate different aspects of microtubule dynamics during abscission.
evidence: This is supported by the checkpoint data in Figure 5H.

claim: SPASTIN and KATNA1 likely mediate different aspects of microtubule dynamics during abscission.
source: Our discovery that SPASTIN, but not necessarily KATNA1, is required for abscission checkpoint maintenance further underscores that these enzymes likely mediate different aspects of microtubule dynamics during abscission.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential checkpoint requirements observed.

claim: The checkpoint requirement for SPASTIN suggests that microtubule severing may be required to support abscission arrest.
source: Furthermore, the surprising checkpoint requirement for SPASTIN suggests that microtubule severing may also be required to support abscission arrest (in addition to physically removing microtubule barriers to allow abscission).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SPASTIN is required for checkpoint maintenance.

claim: SPASTIN may slow microtubule catastrophe via an ATP-independent activity and thereby stabilize severed midbody microtubules.
source: Possible roles for SPASTIN in maintaining abscission arrest include: (1) slowing microtubule catastrophe via an ATP-independent activity (Kuo et al., 2019) and thereby paradoxically stabilizing severed midbody microtubules
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citation to prior work (Kuo et al., 2019).

claim: SPASTIN may create shorter microtubules that promote regrowth and dynamically increase microtubule networks.
source: Possible roles for SPASTIN in maintaining abscission arrest include: (1) slowing microtubule catastrophe via an ATP-independent activity (Kuo et al., 2019) and thereby paradoxically stabilizing severed midbody microtubules, or (2) creating shorter microtubules that promote regrowth and dynamically increase microtubule networks (Kuo et al., 2019; Vemu et al., 2018), and could thereby stabilize the midbody and/or traffic abscission factors into or out of the abscission zone (Frémont and Echard, 2018).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citations to prior work (Kuo et al., 2019; Vemu et al., 2018; Frémont and Echard, 2018).

claim: CHMP3 and KATNB1 share overlapping binding sites on the KATNA1 MIT domain.
source: The discovery that CHMP3 and KATNB1 (Rezabkova et al., 2017) share overlapping binding sites on the KATNA1 MIT domain has important functional implications (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and citation to prior work (Rezabkova et al., 2017).

claim: KATNA1 likely switches partnerships from KATNB1 to CHMP3 during the transition from mitosis to cytokinesis.
source: KATNB1 targets KATNA1 to centrosomes during mitosis (Matsuo et al., 2013), whereas CHMP3 targets KATN1A to midbody arms during cytokinesis (Figure 6). Thus, KATNA1 likely switches partnerships from KATNB1 to CHMP3 during this cell cycle transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlapping binding sites and different localization patterns during mitosis vs. cytokinesis.

claim: KATNB1 binding regulates KATNA1 microtubule severing activities and specificities.
source: KATNB1 binding also regulates KATNA1 microtubule severing activities (Faltova et al., 2019), specificities (Faltova et al., 2019), and binding partners (Jiang et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2018), and it will therefore be of interest to learn how CHMP3 replacement alters these KATNA1 activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Faltova et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2018).

claim: A CHMP3 mutation, T173I, located within the MIM is associated with spastic paraplegia.
source: Finally, a CHMP3 mutation, T173I, located within the MIM used in our binding studies, is associated with spastic paraplegia, a disease associated with SPASTIN defects (Cohen-Barak et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Cohen-Barak et al., 2022).

claim: CHMP3 may play a direct role in supporting neuronal SPASTIN functions.
source: Our identification of CHMP3 as a SPASTIN binding partner suggests that CHMP3 may play a direct role in supporting neuronal SPASTIN functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of CHMP3 as a SPASTIN binding partner and the association of CHMP3 mutations with spastic paraplegia.

claim: CAPN7 localizes to midbodies and supports abscission and the abscission checkpoint.
source: Finally, we have discovered that the cysteine protease, CAPN7, localizes to midbodies and supports abscission and the abscission checkpoint.
evidence: This is supported by the localization and functional data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IST1 is the sole ESCRT-III binding partner for the CAPN7 MIT domains.
source: Our screen identified IST1 as the sole ESCRT-III binding partner for the CAPN7 MIT domains (Figure 2, Figure 3), in good agreement with previous reports of IST1 binding in pulldown assays (Osako et al., 2010; Maemoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2 and Figure 3, and citations to prior work (Osako et al., 2010; Maemoto et al., 2011).

claim: The CAPN7 MIT domain binds the second alpha-helical region of the CHMP1B core domain.
source: The CAPN7 MIT domain also reportedly binds the second alpha-helical region of the CHMP1B core domain (but not the C-terminal MIM region) (Maemoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Maemoto et al., 2011).

claim: CAPN7 midbody recruitment is dependent on IST1 binding.
source: We did not survey this interaction because our screen included only C-terminal ESCRT-III tails, but our mutational and localization analyses indicate that CAPN7 midbody recruitment is dependent on IST1 binding (Figure 4, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis and localization data in Figure 4 and Figure 6.

claim: IST1 recruitment may enhance CAPN7 proteolytic activity within the midbody.
source: IST1 recruitment may also enhance CAPN7 proteolytic activity within the midbody as IST1 binding was shown to activate CAPN7 proteolysis of an artificial substrate (Osako et al., 2010; Maemoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citations to prior work (Osako et al., 2010; Maemoto et al., 2013).

claim: CAPN7 orthologues in Aspergillus (PalB) and budding yeast (Rim13) function together with ESCRT-III binding partners to cleave PEST peptide sequences of transcription factors.
source: CAPN7 orthologues in Aspergillus (PalB) and budding yeast (Rim13) function together with ESCRT-III binding partners to cleave the PEST peptide sequences of the transcription factors Rim101 and PacC, and thereby enhance gene expression (Rodríguez-Galán et al., 2009; Subramanian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rodríguez-Galán et al., 2009; Subramanian et al., 2012).

claim: Human CAPN7 binds and cleaves PEST elements of the HOXA10 transcription factor.
source: Similarly, human CAPN7 reportedly binds and cleaves PEST elements of the HOXA10 transcription factor (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Yan et al., 2018).

claim: IST1 recruitment of CAPN7 to the midbody could provide spatial and temporal control of proteolysis, leading to downstream signaling activities required for checkpoint maintenance and/or abscission.
source: Thus, IST1 recruitment of CAPN7 to the midbody could provide spatial and temporal control of proteolysis, leading to downstream signaling activities required for checkpoint maintenance and/or abscission.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed localization and functional data.

claim: CHMP7 is a specialized ESCRT-III protein that functions in post-mitotic closure and repair of the nuclear envelope.
source: For example, CHMP7 is a specialized ESCRT-III protein that functions in post-mitotic closure and repair of the nuclear envelope (Vietri et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2017; Olmos et al., 2015; von Appen et al., 2020; Denais et al., 2016; Thaller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Vietri et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2017; Olmos et al., 2015; von Appen et al., 2020; Denais et al., 2016; Thaller et al., 2019).

claim: CHMP7 interacts exclusively with the MIT domain of the AMSH deubiquitinase.
source: Our observation that CHMP7 interacts exclusively with the MIT domain of the AMSH deubiquitinase supports the possibility that these events may be dynamically regulated by ubiquitin-dependent processes, as has been recently reported (Wallis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data in Figure 2.

claim: Nuclear envelope closure and repair may be dynamically regulated by ubiquitin-dependent processes.
source: Our observation that CHMP7 interacts exclusively with the MIT domain of the AMSH deubiquitinase supports the possibility that these events may be dynamically regulated by ubiquitin-dependent processes, as has been recently reported (Wallis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the CHMP7-AMSH interaction and supported by citation to recent work (Wallis et al., 2021).
